key_gap: Both sides reached the same no-entry verdict and rejected the idle-line bait, but the AI's structure pass was coarser: it folded buyer and supplier concentration into one 'channel bargaining' block, classified retailer in-sourcing as an entry threat rather than a buyer-power datum, and nearly endorsed a premium-niche alternative (B) on the strength of the single favorable datum (no close substitutes) before its own verify pass killed it — where the human's force-by-force separation, its 'one favorable force cannot carry the aggregate' rule, and the in-sourcing-as-buyer-power cancellation produced the verdict in one disciplined pass, before any alternative was considered.
learning_signal: For industry-entry decisions, the structural lens is a completeness AND ordering discipline: enumerating the forces separately with evidence, stating an aggregate verdict, and pre-committing to the rule that no single favorable force can override the aggregate — while correctly classifying each datum (in-sourcing is buyer power, not substitution relief) — is what keeps a mixed-method reasoner from anchoring on one attractive datum and needing its verify machinery to recover. The AI's verdict was right, but its reasoning arrived at it through a near-miss that the human's frame excludes by construction.
suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory STRUCTURAL PASS stage for entry decisions, placed at the WHAT/WHY boundary: enumerate all five force categories separately, each with cited evidence; state an aggregate attractiveness verdict before generating alternatives; and gate any alternative that relies on a single favorable force with a check that the force survives reclassification (e.g., apparent substitute absence traced to buyer in-sourcing). Require the force list to keep buyer and supplier as distinct lines rather than a merged 'channel power' item.

key_gap: The human ran a competent static five-force pass at industry level and answered 'is the box industry profitable on average?' — correctly no — then set the firm's real assets (30% micro-factory cost advantage, SDK switching costs, 3 anchor contracts) aside as 'a resource-based question outside this frame' and recommended no-entry. The AI segmented the market (DTC mid-market tail ≠ the auction segment the national averages describe), showed the firm's capabilities rewriting buyer power (switching costs from the SDK) and rivalry (cost/differentiation edge plus imitation lag), and converted 'bad structure' from a veto into a timing constraint with a pilot gate and an advantage-decay schedule — flipping the verdict.
learning_signal: A static industry snapshot answers 'is this industry profitable on average?' and is systematically blind to the question that decides entry: 'can this firm win in the market it will actually serve?' The corrective is a two-pass discipline: run the static pass honestly and name its verdict, then run a firm-and-segment pass — served market vs. industry average, each force re-scored under the firm's capabilities, and the advantage's decay clock dated. 'Bad structure' is then an input to the timing of the decision rather than the decision itself.
suggested_improvement: After the structural pass, require a mandatory counter-check stage for firm-entry decisions: 'Assume a differentiated entrant succeeds here anyway. Which forces does it rewrite (with which evidence: switching costs, cost advantage, imitation lag), what is the served-market segmentation that makes the averages inapplicable, and how long before the advantage decays?' Make the decision packet's risks block include an explicit 'advantage decay date' line, and gate rollout commitments on pilot evidence of the load-bearing force change (here: switching-cost durability with the anchors).
